paras: The killing of Henry Allen took place on 5 July 1881 in a harvest field near Mount Sterling, Kentucky, where a Black farm worker named Allen had his throat cut by a man named Freeman. According to a Mount Sterling dispatch, a party came to Allen's house that night to lynch him on an accusation of assaulting a woman, but found him already dead.

The dispatch, dated Mount Sterling, July 6, placed the killing in a harvest field eight miles from the town and called the victim "colored." In its account, Allen had refused to work and threatened Freeman, who then cut his throat. A later brief described the same killing simply as a quarrel between "two harvest hands" in a field near Mt. Sterling on the 5th, after which Allen died of his injuries.

That night, the dispatch said, "parties" went to Allen's house intending to lynch him "for an assault upon a woman." They found him already dead, and the reports neither name the woman nor describe the alleged assault.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of Freeman or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Daily Tribune printed the dispatch on July 7 under the heading "Killed in a Harvest-Field," and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran a condensed version the same day in its "Crime and Disaster" column. Both repeated the lynching party's accusation as its stated reason, without comment.

A week later a syndicated "Tragical Tales" column, carried by the Mower County Transcript in Minnesota and the Watertown Republican and Superior Times in Wisconsin, reduced the story to a single sentence. That version named no race and left out both Allen's alleged threats and the lynching party.

The Tribune called the victim "Honey Allen," while the Intelligencer and the "Tragical Tales" brief gave "Henry Allen," most likely the same man. The killer appears as "Dick Freeman" in the dispatch and as "Slick Freeman" in the brief.

reader.title: Killing of Henry Allen
bases: A single man, Freeman, cut Allen's throat in a harvest-field dispute over work (A1, A2, A3); a party that came to lynch Allen that night found him already dead (A1, A2), so no group violence reached him.

Allen was killed by one man, Freeman, after a quarrel or threats in the field (A1, A3), not by a group acting under a pretext of justice; the 'parties' who came to lynch him for an alleged assault on a woman found him already dead (A1, A2), a lynching threatened but not carried out.

A1 and A2 print the same Mount Sterling dispatch nearly word for word, and the 'Tragical Tales' brief (A3, A4, A5) is a shorter version that agrees on the killing but cannot be shown to be independent; the lynching party appears only in the A1/A2 dispatch.

accounts.label: Mount Sterling dispatch
accounts.gist: Allen, 'colored', refused to work and threatened Freeman, who cut his throat; parties came that night to lynch Allen for an assault upon a woman and found him dead.

accounts.label: 'Tragical Tales' brief
accounts.gist: Two harvest hands, Henry Allen and Slick Freeman, quarreled in a field near Mt. Sterling on the 5th, and Allen died of a throat wound; no race or lynching party is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune ran the dispatch under 'Killed in a Harvest-Field' and the Lancaster Intelligencer in its 'Crime and Disaster' column, both stating the lynching party's accusation without comment.
The 'Tragical Tales' column in Minnesota and Wisconsin weeklies reduced it to a quarrel between 'two harvest hands' with no race named.

conflicts.note: Probably one man; 'Honey' may be a transmission or typesetting error.
The dispatch (A1, A2) is the earlier and more detailed source.
